A crucial challenge in the application of EWCT to holographic quantum error-correcting codes was addressed by the creators of our code. Previous attempts failed due to the non-divisibility of physical degrees of freedom in black holes. A new proposal is introduced to address this problem by assigning divisibility only to the non-extremal entropy of the black hole. This division enables the calculation of the entanglement wedge, which is found to be a finite region of the extended black hole. A new coding scheme is established based on this code, and its properties are studied. A significant finding is that EWCT exhibits a phase transition when the entanglement entropy reaches its extremal state. This transition has a notable application in preserving quantum information within an eternal black hole, as it is found to be possible when the region's size exceeds its horizon.

To achieve this, we employed a grid of 128 simulations for each cloud, varying key parameters such as mass accretion rate, photoevaporation rate, and CO production efficiency, while keeping the initial gas and dust mass fixed. Our simulations revealed that photoevaporation significantly depletes volatile gas, but can also lead to the retention of CO gas, depending on the rate of photoevaporation.

We compared these simulations with observed values from star-forming regions in the literature, and found that most are dominated by CO gas, but exhibit significant gas phase H2O. Our analysis also revealed a correlation between the mass ratio of dust to gas and the distance to its host star, but a weaker correlation than previously reported.

We concluded that photoevaporation can explain the observed dust-to-gas mass ratios, but the effect is highly dependent on the specific conditions of each star-forming region. Our study also has implications for the accuracy of star formation models, as the assumed parameters can significantly affect the predicted mass ratios.

Although automated methods for detecting misinformation have shown promise in recent years, they are often vulnerable to misinformation that has been deliberately concealed within context-specific language. To address this challenge, a novel approach called CoMI-2 is proposed, a context-oriented multi-instance model that effectively aggregates information from multiple language representations to identify misinformation produced through covert prompting techniques. To test the efficacy of this model, a unique dataset called AntiGPT has been created, comprising 1,000 instances generated by the open-source language model GPT-3, including 500 instances of misinformation and 500 control samples, labeled with accompanying context information. Experimental results demonstrate that CoMI-2 significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in misinformation detection, effectively capturing both semantic and syntactic language features and context-oriented information to detect misinformation produced through both covert and overt prompting techniques.

Theoretical models, particularly those involving linear stability analysis and data-driven approaches, are employed to analyze and predict the behavior of ice sheets. By combining data-driven models with linear stability models, it becomes possible to derive the underlying state-space dynamics that drive the observed surface elevation data. This process involves two main steps: first, a data-assimilation approach is used to infer the state-space dynamics from surface elevation data, and second, linear interpolation is used to fill in the missing spatial dimensions of the estimated dynamics. we have determined the spatial distribution of gas velocities in the central regions of two star-forming galaxies, SMM J013629-0010 and SMM J014510-0017. These galaxies, which have gas masses exceeding 10^9 solar masses, exhibit significant central gas reservoirs. Our analysis reveals that these reservoirs, which are larger than the galaxies' star-forming cores, exhibit coherent rotational motion. The central orbits are larger than the galaxies' optical discs, and the outer gas discs exhibit motion patterns distinct from the central discs. Our findings indicate that the central gas discs rotate in a manner similar to that of the galaxies' star-forming cores, and that the outer discs rotate in a manner distinct from the core. 2017-BLG-1440 offers a rare opportunity to study a self-lensing exoplanet system, in which a planet is aligned with its host star to line up directly between the star and Earth. Modal logics, such as modal mu-calculus and a variant called dynamic
modal logic (DMOL), are well-suited for formal verification due to their
integration of efficient model checking techniques and expressive power.
However, traditional model checking approaches have limitations when it
comes to handling DPDL and ADMOL, which are subsets of DPDL-based logics.
This is because they incorporate an additional, more expressive type of
operation - relational programs - in contrast to the Kripke plane-based
programs used in basic modal logic.
To overcome this challenge, we introduce two new models - called 
$\varepsilon$-Kripke planes and 
$\varepsilon$-Kripke frames - that incorporate efficient, bottom-up model
checking procedures for $\varepsilon$-ADMOL and $\varepsilon$-ADMOL with 
completeness, respectively.
These models can efficiently manage large datasets by using an 
incremental approach and memory management.
To demonstrate the effectiveness of our model, we introduce $\varepsilon$-Kripke
Planes, a DPDA-based model-checking tool, and provide experimental results 
showing its superiority over existing model checkers in handling various DPDL 
subsets.

This paper introduces the concept of'strategic equivalence' as a more flexible criterion for rewriting rules, which is less strict than traditional congruence and allows the creation of more effective strategies for program equivalence testing. We specifically focus on a type of rule known as pattern-matching and elimination rules, which replace subprograms with simpler versions, but often fail to support efficient inversion. We then develop a new type of rule, called'strategic-matching and synthesis rules', that maintains an ordering while still allowing efficient reversal. We provide a method for verifying that these rules are strategic by defining inductive synthesis invariants as a way to track the creation of new terms. We use this method to create a model of functional programming called PCF-constructive, which incorporates a form of inductive reasoning that doesn't rely on the principle of excluded middle. We then demonstrate that this model can be used to create a set of effective rewriting strategies that can be used to refactor functional programs.

The number of possible solutions for these puzzles can be calculated by dividing the number of possible input grids by the number of possible grid sizes.  The probability that a random puzzle has a solution can be calculated using Berstein's inequality, which states that the probability of a random puzzle having a solution approaches one as the number of cells in the grid approaches infinity.  The probability that the number of possible solutions deviates from this expectation by at least $\varepsilon$ cells in the grid approaches zero as the number of cells in the grid approaches infinity.  The proof presented in this study relies on results from prior research, which demonstrated that random sparse linear systems over a finite field become unique solution systems as the number of cells in the grid approaches infinity, leading to this new finding.

Traditional reinforcement learning methods, however, often struggle to adapt to these dynamic environments due to the increased sample complexity required for accurate state modeling. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel reinforcement learning algorithm that achieves effective sample usage in textbook examples. we investigate the relationship between an action's value and the beliefs learning agents have about other agents' value functions. We present a method for learning this relationship as a time-dependent correlation coefficient. By focusing on this correlation coefficient, our approach seeks to quantify the degree of dependence between an agent's action value and the product of its belief about another agent's action value and its belief about the other agent's reward function. We define the correlation coefficient to measure how an agent's action choice is dependent on its beliefs, and we analyze the conditions under which this correlation coefficient is well-defined. We also derive a closed-form expression for this correlation coefficient and demonstrate its effectiveness in a variety of multi-agent reinforcement learning tasks. Our results show that this correlation coefficient is a useful tool for understanding the behavior of multi-agent systems and for developing more effective agents.

However, when an entangled state is produced by QND measurement and a common two-mode squeezed vacuum exhibits sub-Poissonian photon counts, it doesn't necessarily indicate a strong correlation between the modes. Conversely, the second method, known as rescaling, modifies smaller events to fit within the desired range, albeit at the expense of event correlations. This paper explores both techniques, in the context of cosmological simulations, for analysing extreme galaxy cluster mergers. It is found that the rescaling approach, despite resampling events multiple times, yields similar results to the cut-off method, which removes events beyond threshold, particularly in terms of merger time sequences and energy release. This similarity allows for the rescaling approach to be a valuable tool for understanding extreme events without limiting the analysis to a fixed threshold level.

One method involves comparing environmental variability across different populations, while the other, two-part test, can be applied within a single population. Our study focuses on the two-part test, assessing two hypotheses about the interaction between genes and environment. Entity Recognition (FGNER) is to identify entities in text and categorize them into predefined categories. Notable FGNER categories include entity types in historical eras, geographic regions, and organism types. Unlike standard Named Entity Recognition (NER), FGNER involves numerous entities within each category, making it a complex task. Current solutions to FGNER either demand substantial training data or employ complex models that struggle with generalizing across entity types. We propose a self-supervised framework called SFGNER that utilizes entity co-occurrence patterns in text to facilitate the learning of representation for each entity type with minimal labeled data. SFGNER's performance significantly surpasses that of baseline algorithms on two benchmark FGNER tasks.

Current data center designs often struggle to maintain optimal performance while minimizing power consumption, a problem that's particularly acute in virtualized environments.  To address this issue, researchers have developed new approaches to manage Data Center Resource Pools (DCRPs) effectively.  Our research explores the potential of DCRP allocation, a strategy that allocates DCRPs to cloud tenants in a way that maximizes their productivity.  By comparing DCRP-based and CPU core-based scheduling methods, we found that the former can reduce power consumption by up to 20% and improve Tenant DCRP Utilization (TDPU) and Power Per Transaction (PPT) metrics.  Additionally, we introduced a new approach called Dynamic Service Chain (DSC) migration, which further optimizes data center performance.  Our experiments demonstrate that DSC migration can reduce power consumption by up to 10% and improve TDPU and PPT metrics.  Overall, our research demonstrates the potential for cloud data centers to achieve significant energy savings and performance improvements through DCRP allocation and DSC migration.

Researchers have long studied adaptive coupling and synchronization in identical units, discovering that the interaction's adaptability can actually promote synchronization. Prior domain adaptation techniques mainly focused on the entire data distribution, using methods like re-weighting, which could not effectively adapt to the varying distribution differences across different data subsets. To address this, a novel adaptation approach called adaptive domain adaptation is proposed, focusing on minimizing distribution discrepancies in specific data subsets. A novel quantization-based method called QADA is proposed to model the entire data's underlying manifold structure, allowing for the identification and adaptation of disparate data subsets. Through a cluster-based data representation, the method enables the adaptive approximation of each data subset's distribution discrepancies in the common latent space, facilitated by a trainable quantization network. theoretical underpinnings of the quantum Rabi model, a foundational system that combines a two-level entity with a single oscillator. The model's development is explored in relation to supersymmetry and the Lie algebra so(2,1), as well as the P\"{o}schl-Teller potential. By quantizing a classical system with the Lie group U(2) \otimes Sp(2, R), a coupled anharmonic oscillator model is derived, which matches the form of the quantum Rabi model. Furthermore, the model can be adapted for use in the Dicke model for multiple two-level entities with a single oscillator. The model is particularly relevant in the strong coupling regime, where quantum phenomena such as anharmonicity and the emergence of spin chains and nanoscale spin qubits can be observed. The text also introduces the quantum Rabi model in the context of circuit quantum electrodynamics, a technology used in superconducting qubits.

researchers are investigating the likelihood of co-orbital planets forming through various migration methods. A key process is the transition from co-orbital to co-planar configurations. Co-planar planets experience orbital phase locking, where their orbits become synchronized due to gravitational interactions. Our study investigates how co-orbital planets can phase lock through a stable central configuration, called an n+1+2 Lagrangian configuration, where the central object, one planet, and the other two planets all orbit each other. We used a novel approach to investigate this phenomenon, where the ratio of distances between the planets and the central object is a specific parameter. Our results show that under certain conditions, the four-body problem can be reduced to a specific type of dynamical system, known as a 2-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian system. By analyzing the changes in this system, we found that an internal bifurcation occurs under specific parameter ranges, leading to a new stable configuration. Our study also used numerical simulations to verify these theoretical predictions. Our findings have potential applications in the study of real planetary systems, where the central object, the two outer planets, and the central object's distance ratio can vary within a specific parameter range.

quantum phase estimation, where a quantum phase is accurately measured by analyzing the evolution of a quantum state. This concept has been adapted into a quantum algorithm for finding the eigenvalues of a matrix, where a simulated quantum process involves applying a specific time-dependent Hamiltonian. By analyzing the resulting eigenstates at a particular time point, where their relative phases are uniform, researchers can use the Ramsey sequence to measure the quantum phase and thereby determine all the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian. This innovation has led to a more accurate algorithm for the data analysis phase of a quantum algorithm for diagonalizing a matrix, reducing its error rate and speeding up its time complexity. Specifically, this new method reduces the time it takes to find an $\epsilon$-accurate eigenvalue from $O(\epsilon^{-1})$ to $O(\epsilon^{-1/2})$. As a direct result, the time it takes to compute a complete eigenvalue spectrum with polynomial accuracy in input size is now possible.

By analyzing a subset of the Coma cluster, we found that outer arms exhibit a preferred elongated shape with alignment and angular orientation consistent with that of their host galaxies. The Coma cluster's inner cores, in contrast, exhibit shape and angular alignment that resemble that of the surrounding galaxies, although this similarity is partly due to varying host galaxy shapes affecting tidal feature morphology. To better understand these features, we developed a model to simulate interactions between galaxies, which accurately replicated observed characteristics of outer arms, but not inner cores. Specifically, it aims to optimize the balance between the economic costs of the pandemic and the costs associated with implementing non-pharmaceutical interventions to limit its spread. By formulating this optimization problem as a dynamic game, the study explores the strategies that different sectors of society might adopt in an effort to minimize their individual losses, resulting in a Nash equilibrium. Our comprehensive analysis of this data, which includes 199 observations over 18 years, reveals a dramatic increase in the galaxy's brightness between 2007 and 2008, which we refer to as the 2007-2008 outburst. To better understand this outburst, we collected an extensive amount of data, which includes 19 spectral and photometric measurements over the course of the outburst. These new findings show that the brightness increase in NGC 4053 was a rapid and dramatic event, with the outburst's main phase lasting approximately 10 months. During this time, the outburst's brightness increased by a factor of 10 in the optical and near-infrared wavelengths. Our analysis of the outburst's spectral energy distribution suggests that the outburst was primarily due to an increase in the accretion rate around the supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center. Our comprehensive dataset and analysis provide valuable insights into the behavior of NGC 4053 during this significant outburst and will serve as a valuable resource for future studies of nuclear galactic nuclei.

To address this issue, we have developed a novel approach called Adversarial Masked Masking (AMM), which enhances the detection of rare objects by incorporating unlabelled images into the training process. The key idea behind this method is to create artificial instances of rare objects in common scenes by adding masks to the images. These masks are then used to mask the mask-added objects and also mask irrelevant areas of the image. The network is trained to remove these masks and restore the original objects and background. Recent studies have shown that the energy cascade is not the only process at play, and that it is also being fed back from dissipation. What drives this energy transfer between scales, however, remains unclear.

We have found that the energy cascade in three-dimensional rotating turbulence is driven by a combination of factors, including both the rotation of the fluid and fluctuations in velocity. These factors contribute to a transfer of energy from large to small scales, and vice versa, and their relative importance varies depending on the specific conditions of the flow.

Our findings reveal that the energy transfer is not solely dependent on the rotation of the fluid, but also on velocity fluctuations, and that the energy transfer is more efficient when the flow is both rotating and has small-scale velocity fluctuations.

These results have important implications for our understanding of three-dimensional rotating turbulence, and may help to clarify some of the remaining mysteries of this complex flow.

BY Deneva is a BY Draconis star, characterized by a strong magnetic field, and its spectrum has been observed to exhibit a broad 14.2 GHz emission feature.  This emission feature has been detected in both X-ray and radio bands, and its variability has been observed to occur on a timescale of days to weeks.  Our analysis of the spectral energy distribution of BY Deneva has led us to conclude that this emission feature is an Alfvén wave.  Our findings also suggest that a helical Alfvén wave is more consistent with the observed properties of the emission feature than a toroidal wave, and that the energy of the wave is generated at the star's surface and decays as it propagates through the stellar atmosphere.  Our study also reveals that a similar type of emission feature is likely to be present in other stars in the BY Draconis class, and that these emissions may be a result of energy transfer from the star's core to its atmosphere, and that this energy may be responsible for driving stellar winds.

recommendations are gaining significant attention due to their exceptional performance in various real-world applications. The conventional view that the transverse single-nucleon electromagnetic current is incoherent with the pion field is refuted. The skeleton approach instead considers a unified, coherent picture where the transverse single-pion current is linked with the pion's electromagnetic form factor. The term "skeleton" in this context refers to the nucleon entity, which may be a three-quark baryon or a five-quark $q^6$ baryon, arising in quark-coalescence processes. Neural Networks (DCNNs), have achieved remarkable success in computer vision, but their vulnerability to malicious inputs has been a significant concern. Malicious inputs, crafted through adversarial attacks, can cause the models to misinterpret images, leading to a failure in recognizing them. This paper introduces a method to bolster the resilience of DCNNs against adversarial attacks by augmenting the training dataset with artificially generated perturbations. By applying this technique to a state-of-the-art DCNN, we have demonstrated its ability to improve the accuracy of adversarial training and reduce attack success rates. Our experiments indicate that this method can significantly enhance the robustness of DCNNs, as evidenced by the results on the ImageNet dataset using adversarial perturbations.

Utilizing these data, we determine the star's period and analyze its variability, employing the Wilson-Davis-Keller model to simulate its light variations. imate near-duplicate problem is an approximation version of the approximate near-duplicate problem where the distance metric used is the continuous Fréchet distance. Near-duplicates are defined as subdivisions of two inputs, where the first is a collection of p polygons and the second is of two collections of polygons with quantity p and s respectively, where the distance between the subdivisions is at most k and the quantity s does not exceed a value of k to the power of some constant. It has been found that the problem has an time limit of O((k * (p + s)) * (p + n)/epsilon) where n is the total quantity of vertices in the input collections and the result holds for an epsilon that is at least 0.1. The result improves upon an earlier algorithm that had a time limit of O((p + n)/epsilon) for the case where s equals 0 and is comparable to the results found for other approximation versions of the near-duplicate problem that use the discrete Fréchet distance. The result builds upon an algorithm proposed by Arikovska et al. and uses the same data structure developed in their work as the first step. The algorithm then uses a second step to find a matching of vertices in the two input collections that is close enough to the optimal result. The algorithm has been tested on various types of data and the results show that it performs well.

Health Records (EHRs) has been extensively explored by researchers.  A key challenge in this process lies in identifying relevant time points within clinical events, known as temporal event extraction (TEE).  Existing TEE methods, however, often lack a unified framework for extracting events and timing, making full event extraction (EE) difficult to achieve.  To address this challenge, we propose the Event Extraction with Temporal Event Extraction (EE-TEE) framework, which combines event extraction (EE) and temporal event extraction (TEE) to enable more effective event extraction.  By using a time-aware cross-attention mechanism within the TEE task, we enable full event extraction through mutual guidance.  Experimental results on the T54 dataset demonstrate that our EE-TEE task significantly outperforms traditional full event extraction, with a +2.11 improvement in F1-score over the current best baseline.

Speech Recognition (ASR) has yielded impressive results, but a single direction of time-feeds is insufficient to fully capture time patterns. Time-feeds in both time and time-frequency dimensions have thus been implemented. When a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) processes time-patterns, its filters also need spatial invariance, achieved through Local Response Normalization (LRN). However, this technique may hinder the exploration of various time-patterns due to its restrictive nature. In our research, we investigated the impact of time-patterns on speech recognition accuracy when combined with DNNs, and found that a balance between time-patterns and LRN is necessary. We discovered that a modest introduction of global time-patterns can enhance recognition accuracy, particularly when paired with advanced architectures such as bidirectional and multi-filter/layer settings. Our experiments were conducted on the Google Web Search (WES) dataset, a large-scale system with over 100,000 units, and a 24.8% word error rate.

Networks can be found in various forms, such as social networks, biological networks, and technological networks. tool for analyzing the production and decay of complex leptoquark scenarios involving lepton flavor violation. This particular study delves into an unsupervised learning approach that enables the categorization of industries according to their behavior in contrast to their respective benchmark S&P 500 portfolios. The proposed method begins by segmenting each sector into distinct groups based on its composition, subsequently removing non-significant stocks. The remaining representative stocks in each sector are then transformed into binary sequences, indicating whether a stock is part of the corresponding benchmark portfolio or not. The binary sequences for each sector are aggregated to create a corresponding S&P 500 benchmark portfolio sequence. The method then computes sequence-derived features, including the number of ones, the distribution of ones, and the length of consecutive segments. The method finally applies a clustering algorithm to group industries based on sequence-derived features. The proposed clustering approach demonstrates superior performance compared to alternative methods in evaluating sector performance.

A novel approach called the Local Barrier Removal (LBR) method achieves this by eliminating the need for a global barrier check across all threads. Developed in the 1990s, this technique initially focused on reducing a single global barrier but has now been expanded to incorporate a more comprehensive strategy. By utilizing a two-level program structure, where the lower level contains non-barrier code and waits at individual barriers, and the lower level's threads synchronize at fast barrier points, LBR allows for an n-fold speedup compared to traditional methods. A key feature of LBR is its ability to defer synchronization at fast barrier points until a slow barrier is encountered, resulting in an overall speedup equivalent to n+1. Furthermore, LBR can be applied to a range of existing parallel algorithms, including a matrix multiplication algorithm, to optimize performance.

In this study, we present ADLKA, a method for producing lightweight student models by utilizing a more powerful teacher model as a reference. Our method operates in two stages: initially, a universal space is created through the teacher model to accommodate a specific language, and subsequently, a student model is developed to replicate the teacher model's behavior. Our method's ability to successfully learn from complex teacher models is demonstrated through its ability to do so from a character-based ELMo model, and our method's effectiveness is further highlighted by its ability to match the performance of a character-based BERT model and surpass other knowledge distillation techniques when trained on a character-based BERT teacher model.

medical image processing is heavily dependent on the quality of the training data. Nonetheless, obtaining semantic segmentation labels for medical images is a labor-intensive process requiring expert knowledge. In this paper, we propose an innovative method for refining semantic segmentation labels by combining the strengths of various established algorithms. By integrating the efficiency of the most effective and reliable methods, such as the Label Refinement using Iterative Refinement (LIRI) algorithm and the Label Refinement using Iterative Refinement with Context (LIRIC) algorithm, our approach, known as Label Refinement using Iterative Refinement with Context (LIRIC), achieves a balance between improved accuracy and reduced processing time. Our method's performance is demonstrated by comparing it to the state-of-the-art algorithms on the ISIC17 and ISIC18 datasets, with results showing that our approach outperforms the compared methods in terms of both improved segmentation accuracy and decreased processing time.

To address this issue, a game-theoretic model is proposed to examine the interactions between a defender and an adversary in a scenario involving the use of autonomous agents, either artificial intelligence or robotics. By employing a game-theoretic approach, optimal strategies can be determined for both the defender and the adversary to either minimize losses or maximize their benefits. This problem is analogous to a card game in which both the defender and the adversary have a limited budget to allocate their resources efficiently. To solve this complex issue, a type of Markov decision process is utilized to find optimal policies that minimize long-term losses. A learning algorithm is proposed to help the defender and the adversary find optimal strategies through trial and error, allowing them to adjust their actions based on their experiences. This learning algorithm is theoretically proven to converge to optimal policies, ensuring the best possible outcomes. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, it is tested on a complex scenario and compared to alternative methods.

This research investigates the effectiveness of neural network-based techniques for predicting day-ahead electricity usage at the individual feeder level within a large Canadian utility. In this context, a new method has been developed to evaluate the fairness of high school students' mathematical assessments that utilize the K12 AI platform. The electron pressure gradient term is the next most significant contribution, which is included when going beyond the fluid model. Our study examines how the inclusion of higher-order terms affects the free energy balance, which reveals that the collisional operator is more complex than the simple, primary term suggests. The presence of additional, primary term-independent components can lead to either the generation or the return of energy, either to the electrons or to the magnetic field. The direction of energy flow is determined by the interplay of multiple factors, which are not present in the primary term. To investigate this, we have developed a method to calculate the eigenvalue spectrum of the free energy operator, which takes into account the influence of the primary term, including its sign-dependent effects, and determines the direction of energy flow in a given plasma scenario.

To address these issues, a new approach called large image memory (LIM) is proposed, which combines a multi-component system with a query re-ranking module to optimize image retrieval.
The LIM architecture consists of a query encoding module, a coarse image memory, a re-ranking module, an image encoding memory, a candidate selection module, and a final re-ranking module.
Each component plays a crucial role in enhancing the overall image retrieval process.
The query encoding module generates a compact, semantically rich query embedding, which is then used to activate the coarse image memory.
A coarse image memory stores a reduced set of candidate images, allowing the system to reduce the search space and improve efficiency.
A candidate selection module then uses a cross-modal attention mechanism to select a reduced set of relevant images, which are further re-ranked by a final re-ranking module to produce the final search results.
Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed LIM architecture outperforms state-of-the-art search techniques and achieves significant improvements in image retrieval performance.

However, this assumption is invalid for images with intensity variations, such as those resulting from deformations. To address this issue, a novel cost function is proposed for computing multiple registrations between a set of images. This cost function takes into account not only intensity values but also the average intensity of the corresponding patch under each estimated transformation. By incorporating this approach, it is demonstrated that the matching cost can effectively identify the correct transformation. Additionally, a fast and efficient algorithm is developed to compute these integrations.

, the non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) technique has been suggested to enhance spectral efficiency and connectivity capacity. Future wireless networks will likely integrate NOMA with existing WiFi to provide high-quality services. To achieve this, we developed and tested a real-time NOMA solution for WiFi by combining the orthogonal frequency division multiple access (OFDMA) and greedy power allocation (GPA) methods. To verify its effectiveness, we created simulation models and measured the results, finding the NOMA solution provided additional connectivity and a performance gain. Furthermore, due to its ad-hoc nature, the NOMA solution can be used immediately without interference with existing WiFi networks, allowing for flexible deployment and potential improvements in performance.
